column4: All are brought into view with nothing concealed; this ayah introduces the public judgment scene before the next ayah assigns the book to the right hand, and it echoes the section’s challenged claim that no one sees.
The human is described as laboring toward the Lord and meeting Him; this opens the same book-and-destination scene with effort leading to encounter.
The person later handed his book behind his back had been joyful among his people; this gives the worldly stance that precedes his false expectation in the next ayah.
He thought he would never return to God; this is a specific false expectation opposite the right-hand recipient’s expectation in 69:20 and the section’s mistaken assumption in 90:5.
His Lord had been watching him; this completes the false-return scene and answers the section’s 90:7 question about whether anyone sees.

Each person’s lot or record is fastened to that person’s neck; the attachment concretely parallels the section’s gloss of أصحاب as those who stay attached to a side, though this ayah does not name either side.
The person is told to read his record and is his own reckoner; this completes the preceding image of an individual record attached to its bearer.

The scripture’s inheritors are divided into three moral classes, from those wronging themselves to those foremost in good; this is another concrete triad beside the section’s cited three classes in 56:7 and its two named sides.

Believers are brought from darkness into light, while disbelievers are brought from light into darkness and become lasting companions of the Fire; this joins the section’s right-light and adverse-side associations in a distinct paired formulation.

Those who disbelieve and deny the signs are companions of the Fire, abiding there; this closely restates the section’s denial-of-signs group and supports its gloss of companions as residents attached to a side.
Created shadows incline to the right and left while prostrating; this makes right and left tangible as directions, though the ayah describes shadows rather than human moral groups.
Iblis says he will sit against people on God’s straight path; this sets up the section’s image of guidance and chosen ways as a contest over direction.
Iblis says he will approach people from before, behind, right, and left; this is a hostile use of side-directions around the guided path, not the final two groups, and continues the preceding threat.
The one who gives and is mindful of God takes the favorable course; this parallels the compassionate good deeds preceding the right-side group.
The giver affirms the good; this makes the positive course a matter of belief as well as action.
God eases that person toward ease; the chosen course reaches a fitting end, clarifying the section’s road-to-destination image.
The opposing person withholds and feels self-sufficient; this reverses the generosity and humility associated with the favorable side.
That person denies the good; this parallels the denial that defines the section’s adverse group.
God eases the withholding denier toward hardship; this gives the other course its distinct destination.
His wealth will not avail when he falls; this gives a specific limit to worldly possession on the adverse course.
God declares that guidance is His responsibility; this frames the two courses in the preceding and following ayat as guidance.
The first life and the Hereafter belong to God; this completes the guidance frame with the final domain of the two courses.
The surah warns of a blazing Fire; this gives the adverse course a concrete end like the fire over the section’s left-side people.
Only the most wretched will burn in that Fire; this identifies the condemned class following the warning.
The condemned person denies and turns away; this concretely matches the rejection associated with the adverse side.
The most God-fearing are kept away from the Fire; this is the positive group’s explicit opposite outcome.
The God-fearing person gives wealth to purify himself; this links a concrete act of giving to the favorable end.
His giving is not repayment of another’s favor; this specifies the motive behind the positive course.
He seeks only his Lord’s countenance; this completes the motive of the giving.
He will be satisfied; this closes the positive course with its promised outcome.
Humanity is guided to a way, then becomes grateful or ungrateful; this directly links the section’s two guided roads with the two kinds of people who reach its sides.
For the ungrateful, the next ayah names chains, shackles, and a blaze; this gives the adverse road a concrete punishment.
The righteous are introduced with a drink of camphor; this begins the positive group’s reward scene.
The righteous fulfill vows and fear a day whose evil spreads widely; this describes the conduct and judgment-awareness of the positive group.
They give food to the needy, orphan, and captive despite wanting it themselves; this is a direct parallel to the section’s feeding of the orphan and poor before the right-side label.
They say they feed only for God, seeking neither repayment nor thanks; this specifies the motive of the compassionate act.
They fear a severe day from their Lord; this continues the good group’s stance toward the judgment that divides the sides.
God protects them from that day’s evil and gives them joy; this supplies the outcome of their stance.
Their patience is rewarded with a Garden and silk; this completes the positive group’s path with a lasting place.
Those whose scales are heavy receive a favorable outcome; this is a measured division of people into distinct final conditions.
The heavy-scaled person is in a pleasing life; this gives the favorable side a lived destination.
Those whose scales are light face the opposite outcome; the verse marks the other side of the measure.
The light-scaled person’s destination is the abyss; this names the adverse place.
The abyss is identified as a blazing Fire; this completes the measured division with the adverse destination named in the section.
